hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 and the note about land bridges 20 000 years ago - what separates Bali, Java and Sumatra now, and what does that stop tigers doing?
Think about what is different on each separate island that could act on variation - climate, prey, habitat and random changes in DNA.
Recall how natural selection works when some individuals have an allele that helps them survive and breed better than others.
Link long time periods with no interbreeding to the build-up of genetic differences and the name for speciation by geographic separation.
walkthrough:
Start With Separation By Sea**
Tigers once could move when land bridges connected the islands, but now sea separates Bali, Java and Sumatra. That is geographical isolation, so tigers on one island cannot breed with tigers on another and there is no gene flow to mix alleles.

Different Islands Mean Different Evolution**
Each island has its own environmental conditions and selection pressures, and different random mutations arise in each isolated population. Some mutations produce alleles that make a tiger better adapted to its own island.

Natural Selection Builds Up Differences**
Better adapted individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce, so they pass those advantageous alleles to offspring. Over many generations the frequency of those alleles rises separately on each island.

From Subspecies Toward New Species**
Because the gene pools stay separate, genetic differences accumulate. The populations show phenotypic differences but can still potentially interbreed, so they are subspecies formed by allopatric speciation, the early stage of reproductive isolation.

Final answer: Geographical isolation by sea between islands with no gene flow / interbreeding between populations; different selection pressures / environmental conditions and different mutations on each island; individuals with advantageous alleles survive, reproduce and pass on alleles; over many generations populations become reproductively isolated by allopatric speciation.

hints: Remember what a primer does in PCR - what part of the DNA mixture does it attach to before DNA polymerase can work?
Think why you would want to copy only the useful evolutionary sections of mtDNA, not all the DNA from a museum sample, and what comparing those sections tells you.
walkthrough:
Primers Pick The Right Piece**
A primer is a short single strand of DNA that binds by complementary base pairing to a matching sequence. Using primers matching tiger mtDNA means DNA polymerase starts copying only at those places.

Copy Only What You Want To Compare**
Museum samples contain mixed and degraded DNA. Specific primers ensure only the useful mtDNA sections for evolution studies are amplified in large amounts, so the sequences from different subspecies can be compared to judge relatedness.

Final answer: Primers bind to complementary base sequences in tiger mtDNA so only the specific target mtDNA sections are amplified; differences / similarities in these sections are then compared to assess how closely related the subspecies are.

hints: Compare one nucleus with many mitochondria in a cell - which type of DNA will there be far more copies of, especially in old museum material?
Link that abundance to the practical job of getting enough DNA to run PCR and sequence successfully.
walkthrough:
Lots Of Copies In Every Cell**
Each cell has one nucleus with nuclear DNA but hundreds of mitochondria, each with its own small circular mtDNA. So there are very many copies of mtDNA per cell.

Why That Helps Evolutionary Work**
More starting copies means it is much easier to extract enough DNA and get successful PCR amplification, which is vital when DNA from museum specimens is old and degraded. Any one valid pair is enough, for example small genome makes it easier to locate target sections, maternal inheritance gives a clear lineage, or higher mutation rate gives a faster molecular clock.

Final answer: Large quantity of mtDNA per cell as many mitochondria per cell / many copies per mitochondrion; so easier to extract and amplify sufficient DNA for testing, especially from old museum specimens.

hints: Think about what happens on small crowded islands in the 20th Century when human populations grow and forests are cleared.
Think about direct human threats to large predators and indirect threats through their food supply or disease.
walkthrough:
Loss Of Space And Food**
On small islands like Bali and Java, forest clearance for farming and settlements causes habitat loss. That also reduces prey animals and increases competition for space and mates, so small tiger populations cannot survive.

Direct Human Pressure**
Large predators are also vulnerable to hunting, poaching and poisoning by humans, plus disease can wipe out a small isolated population quickly. Any two of these pressures explain extinction in the 20th Century.
Final answer: Any two from: habitat loss; increased competition for space / mates; reduction in prey; poaching / hunting / poisoning by humans; disease.

hints: Recall the definition given at the start - a subspecies is genetically distinct and looks a bit different but is not yet reproductively isolated.
Think of the two main tests for staying in the same species - how similar they look, work and are in DNA, and what would happen if they bred with mainland tigers.
walkthrough:
Still Very Similar**
P. t. sumatrae is described as the closest living relative of the extinct island tigers and its mtDNA is very similar to other tigers. It still shares most morphological, physiological, behavioural and biochemical features and much of its DNA with mainland Panthera tigris.

The Breeding Test For A Species**
The key biological idea is reproductive isolation. Because it is only a subspecies, it could still interbreed with mainland tigers to give fertile offspring, so it has not separated enough to be a different species.

Final answer: Any two from: morphologically / physiologically / behaviourally / biochemically similar to mainland tigers Panthera tigris; genetically similar to mainland tigers; could breed with mainland tigers to produce fertile offspring so not reproductively isolated.
